passage: Note from Avni, school counsellor. At Thursday's parent meeting, Jomon sat with his son Rohit's report and said, more than once, "The neighbour's boy already has a rank in the top ten. Why can't he do the same?" His jaw was tight, and he kept turning his pen. When I asked what he was hoping for, he said, "I wanted to study engineering and never could. I don't want Rohit to end up behind like me." He looked surprised at his own words. I asked what Rohit hears when he says it. After a pause, Jomon said, "Probably that he isn't enough." What I did: I suggested he name one thing Rohit really worked at, and he mentioned the neat maths notebook Rohit had kept up for a month. He wrote it down to say at home.

qa.q: What did Jomon say the neighbour's boy already had?
qa.a: He said the neighbour's boy already had a rank in the top ten.

qa.q: What was Jomon afraid of when he compared Rohit to the neighbour's boy?
qa.a: He was afraid Rohit would fall behind as he felt he had, and his own regret over engineering sat under the comparison.

qa.q: What could Jomon do at home that would motivate Rohit better than comparing?
qa.a: He could praise real effort, such as the neat maths notebook, so Rohit knows his father sees the work he does.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel hearing his father's comparison?
qa.a: Probably that he isn't enough, as Jomon himself guessed, which could make love feel conditional on results.

grounding: Shows a parent comparing his child from fear and regret, seen by a counsellor who helps him notice and praise real effort.

passage:
Tuesday, late.
Rukmini came home with her maths test today. Seventy-one. Before I could stop myself I said, "Mitra's daughter got ninety-four, you know." Her face shut like a door. She said, "Baba, you always do this," and went to her room without dinner.
I sat with the paper and heard my own father's voice coming out of me. At her age I dropped out of engineering coaching, and some part of me still burns about it. I'm scared she will carry the same regret. That fear is mine, not hers.
The comparison did nothing for her. It only taught her that my warmth depends on a number.
Tomorrow at breakfast I'll tell her I saw her redo the geometry chapter alone on Sunday. That effort was real. I want her to hear that first.
— Anirban

qa.q: What mark did Rukmini get on her maths test?
What was Anirban feeling after Rukmini left the table?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid: ashamed that he sounded like his own father, and afraid that Rukmini would carry the same regret he still carries.

qa.q: What does Anirban plan to do differently at breakfast?
qa.a: He plans to praise the real effort he saw, Rukmini redoing the geometry chapter alone, before any talk of marks.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see her Baba's comparison?
qa.a: She likely hears that his love depends on her score, which is why she shut down and skipped dinner instead of trying harder.

grounding: A parent notices that comparing his daughter comes from his own regret and fear, and chooses to praise her effort instead.

Darshan: no. it makes me want to stop trying
Keerthana: Then I'm done with it. I saw you redo that chemistry chapter three times this week. That took real grit.
Darshan: ok
Darshan: can you save me some rice
Keerthana: Already in the oven ❤️

qa.q: Which chapter did Darshan redo three times this week?
What was Keerthana worried about while comparing Darshan with Sid?
qa.a: Keerthana was anxious that Darshan would end up with the same regret Keerthana still feels about leaving the science stream.

qa.q: Which choice worked in this chat, and why?
qa.a: Keerthana owned her regret, stopped the comparison and named Darshan's real effort; that let Darshan relax enough to ask for food.

qa.q: How does Darshan see the comparisons with Sid?
qa.a: To Darshan they feel like a message of never being enough, and they make Darshan want to stop trying rather than work harder.

grounding: A mother admits her comparisons come from her own regret, stops them, and praises her child's real effort instead.
